BOI.name: Boise
BOI.excerpt: As the next trough approaches our area Friday, precipitation chances will begin to increase across higher terrain in SW-Idaho Friday afternoon.

sections.name: Key Messages
paragraphs: - Isolated to scattered showers today, greatest coverage northern mountain zones. minor snow accumulations above 6000 ft MSL.
- Gradual clearing this evening. With temperatures around 5 degrees below normal through Wednesday.
- Dry and warmer Thursday, precipitation chances increasing Friday into the weekend.

sections.name: Short Term
paragraphs: Isolated to scattered showers will continue today as a secondary wave and weak cold front cross over the area, especially this afternoon with daytime heating aiding in destabilization. The highest coverage of showers will fall over our northern mountain zones (30-60%), and eastern Oregon (10-20%). Chances in SW Idaho are under 10%, but a shower here or there isn't out of question. Weak instability this afternoon will allow showers to take on a convective nature, with rain and graupel at lower elevations and isolated lightning flashes possible (chances less than 10%). Snow levels this afternoon will range from 4.5-6.5 kft MSL, increasing from northwest to southeast. Showers will linger in our northern zones tonight, tapering off through Wednesday. Areas of clearing tonight will allow for areas of fog development, especially in sheltered mountain valleys; this threat will repeat itself each night through the short-term period. Temperatures this afternoon and next will be in the 50s in the Snake Plain, 40s in the Oregon high desert, higher Idaho basins, and mountain valleys. A cooling trend in overnight lows will set in, with lows Thursday morning near 30 degrees throughout lower elevations and 10-20 degrees in the Oregon high desert and higher Idaho basins.

Thursday will be dry across the area with increasing southwesterly flow ahead of the next system. With a more southerly component in the flow, temperatures Thursday afternoon will be around 5 degrees warmer than that of today and Wednesday.

sections.name: Long Term
paragraphs: As the next trough approaches our area Friday, precipitation chances will begin to increase across higher terrain in SW-Idaho Friday afternoon. This will ring true come Saturday afternoon, except precipitation chances will continue to increase through the day Sunday (mainly across southwest Idaho) as the trough and it's associated cold front cross the area. The southwesterly flow aloft will keep snow levels at 5-7 kft MSL (rising as you move from west to east). This should keep the majority of snow accumulations above 6kft MSL (a 30-50% chance of exceeding 2 inches of snow Saturday afternoon through Sunday, chances increasing with elevation). While snow levels lower following the frontal passage, this will also be about the time precipitation begins tapering off. The area will dry out Monday as upper level ridging builds in behind the departing trough. Dry conditions will prevail through the beginning of next week. Seasonable or below normal temperatures will continue through the long-term period.

BOU.name: Boulder / Denver
BOU.excerpt: A stronger, more organized system could approach the region by the end of the weekend into next week. A strong upper trough is projected to crash southeastward towards our forecast area, potentially interacting with the moist subtropical jet streak.

sections.name: Key Messages
paragraphs: - Warmer and mostly dry much of this week.
- Unsettled weather potentially returning late in the weekend and early next week, with a 20-30% chance of season's first snow in lower elevations towards next Tuesday.

sections.name: Update
paragraphs: Dense fog has developed overnight across the plains, with visibility dropping as low as 1/4 mile in some locations. A Dense Fog Advisory is in place until 9AM for the I-25 corridor and adjacent plains, and until 10AM for the northeast corner, with hazardous travel conditions expected for the morning commute. Take it slow out there and remember to use your low beams!

sections.name: Discussion
paragraphs: It's relatively quiet across the forecast area this evening. We're just starting to see the first bit of fog/mist develop across Lincoln county, and stratus/mist has slowly developed along the northwest Denver metro/northern I-25 corridor over the past couple of hours. We still expect fog to become more widespread across the plains overnight tonight, with some dense fog likely over portions of the I-25 corridor later tonight through the AM commute Tuesday. Some dense fog advisories may be needed overnight, but would like to see the fog actually develop before trying to pinpoint where the dense fog is compared to the less impactful low stratus.

Fog and stratus should erode pretty quickly during the morning hours Tuesday. Like today, temperatures will be slow to warm up during the day, with highs generally in the low to mid 60s - potentially a bit cooler for the northern I-25 corridor.

The rest of the upcoming week looks quiet, as dry west/southwesterly flow aloft continues. A return to a more active pattern begins towards the end of this week or this weekend. A weak but well-defined shortwave lifts north out of New Mexico into the central Great Plains on Friday. It looks like this will track just to the east of our forecast area, but there should be an increase in cloud cover along with a chance of showers along the far eastern plains, with better chances in Kansas/Nebraska. Around the same time, some moisture from the Pacific reaches western Colorado either Friday or Saturday, leading to some scattered light rain/snow showers across the mountains to start the weekend.

A stronger, more organized system could approach the region by the end of the weekend into next week. A strong upper trough is projected to crash southeastward towards our forecast area, potentially interacting with the moist subtropical jet streak. As the previous shift noted, there is quite a bit of spread across guidance. Several of deterministic models over the last 12 hours have advertised the idea of a stronger upper low moving across Colorado, though many still remain rather quiet across the state with a disorganized trough quickly moving through. Ensemble guidance continues to show a wide distribution of solutions, ranging from almost no precip in our CWA to some rather juicy (and at times, snowy) scenarios. Within the ensemble distribution, there has not been a significant trend in any direction. Given that we're still several days out, most of these cycle to cycle changes are simply noise, and it will take some time before a clear trend emerges. Still, it's worth monitoring for the few days in an otherwise quite forecast period.

CYS.name: Cheyenne
CYS.excerpt: While the longer range models had some significant timing differences with the upper-level shortwave moving through, the GFS and ECMWF are in good agreement with the progression of the incoming upper-level trough.

sections.name: Key Messages
paragraphs: - Drier and warmer, but windier conditions are expected Tuesday into Wednesday with a low potential for High Wind criteria being met for the wind-prone areas along the I-80 corridor.
- Quieter weather to end the week, but multiple systems are taking shape for the weekend into the start of next week. At this time, model agreement is poor so confidence is low.

sections.name: Short Term
paragraphs: The system that brought SE Wyoming and the Nebraska Panhandle some beneficial moisture earlier today has since moved off to the north and east, leaving us in a much calmer pattern over the next few days. Gauge observations along with MRMS QPE shows totals as high as 0.75" across mainly the southern portion of the Panhandle, with lighter amounts up to 0.25" across SE Wyoming.

Surface observations at this hour continue to show weak low-level upslope flow in a rather moist air mass, resulting in areas of dense fog mainly east of the Laramie Range. Have decided to issue a Dense Fog Advisory until 9AM MDT for the I-80 corridor including the summit and points east, in addition to the I-25 corridor where visibilities less than 1/4 mile have been observed. Low-level moisture is expected to mix out sometime mid-morning thanks to an increase in our winds (i.e. mechanical turbulence), and any lingering fog should dissipate. Tuesday will feature dry conditions and warmer temperatures relative today ahead of an amplifying wave located off the Pacific Northwest, placing us under WSW flow aloft. Expect highs to be around 5-10 degrees above average east of the I- 25, mainly in the low to mid 60s, with slightly cooler 50s to the west of the Laramie Range. Aside from the notable warming and clearing relative to the previous couple of days, most will also notice an uptick in our winds. This will occur as a deeper closed low phases with a weaker shortwave trough to our north and west, increasing the height gradient and therefore our mid-level flow. Westerly 700 mb flow is expected to ramp up to 45-50 knots through Tuesday morning, with a strong mountain wave signature showing up on the omega fields, mainly across the Snowy Range and to a lesser extent the Laramie Range. One limiting factor that will make this more of a marginal high wind event, rather than a slam dunk, will be the lack of a mountain top stable layer, as model cross-sections aren't showing a tight vertical isentropic gradient (i.e lack of static stability) at mountain top. In-house random forest guidance currently has Arlington with a 40% probability of high wind conditions sometime mid-morning, with Bordeaux at around 20%. Due to the somewhat marginal high wind setup and relatively low confidence, decided to keep the High Wind Watch going until 12PM MDT for the wind-prone areas of the Snowy Range, along with northern portions of Converse County. Decided to nudge up the wind speeds through Tuesday morning from the NBM by going with a blend of the NBM 90th percentile combined with CONS MOS to match the more probable wind gusts up to 50-55 mph for Arlington and other wind-prone areas along the I-80 corridor.

Expect a seasonably chilly, but dry night Tuesday into Wednesday with lows mainly in the 30s and breezy conditions west of the Laramie Range. With much lighter winds to the east of the I-25 corridor, along with high-resolution ensemble guidance having median RH values above 90% in the Panhandle, areas of fog into Wednesday morning are also possible, especially with the recent increase in soil moisture from the past system.

The warming trend will continue into Wednesday as upper-level ridging gradually builds across the eastern half of the country. Under subsidence, cross-barrier flow (albeit weaker than Tuesday), and downsloping, can expect another day with above-average temperatures with highs mainly in the 60s east of the I-25 corridor, and 50s to the west. Conditions will also be breezy across SE Wyoming, although most likely below high wind criteria as surface gradient flow weakens and a rather weak surface low translates to the north and east over the Dakotas. Overnight Wednesday will be much like Tuesday night, although perhaps slightly cooler with a lack of low clouds and light winds. Most locations should hover just above freezing waking up on Thursday, although the usual cool spots of Laramie and Alliance dip down to or slightly below the freezing mark.

sections.name: Long Term
paragraphs: Mostly quiet weather expected to start the long term forecast as upper-level flow turns west-southwesterly and weakens for Thursday. The next upper-level trough will start to become more amplified off the coast of the Pacific Northwest throughout the day Thursday, while a shortwave develops off the coast of central California. Expecting a nice day on Thursday with highs in the upper-50s to upper-60s across the region with sunny skies turning partly cloudy into the overnight hours. The aforementioned upper-level shortwave will move quickly to the northeast Thursday into Friday as it moves inland with long range models currently suggesting it will impact the region late Friday evening into the overnight hours. However, there is some model disagreement on how quick this shortwave ejects northward. The GFS suggests the shortwave moving through between 06 and 18Z on Saturday, while the ECMWF suggest delayed impact between 18 Saturday and 06Z Sunday. Precipitation chances are anticipated with the passage of the shortwave, with isolated showers possible across the Panhandle as early as 18Z Friday, but a delayed shortwave would delay the increasing precipitation chances across the region. Clouds will accompany this shortwave, with mostly cloudy skies expected throughout the day Friday as the shortwave approaches the region. Friday will be mild with temperatures in the low- to mid-60s everywhere.

While the longer range models had some significant timing differences with the upper-level shortwave moving through, the GFS and ECMWF are in good agreement with the progression of the incoming upper-level trough. This trough is currently progged to move inland Saturday evening, strengthening as it does so. The CWA is progged to be caught between the Sub-Tropical jet across the southern half of the CONUS and the incoming Polar Jet across the northern half of the CWA. As a result, a brief period of zonal flow is anticipated early Sunday morning before upper-level winds turn southwesterly with the approaching system. Monday onwards, long range models start to diverge once again with the GFS suggesting the upper-level low diving southward into northern New Mexico. The ECMWF on the other hand broadens the low and advects it directly overhead, before elongating the trough southward Tuesday morning. Both evolutions would bring widespread precipitation into the region Monday and Tuesday, but the ECMWF evolution would keep precipitation around longer, likely leading to higher accumulation values. Another glaring difference between the GFS and the ECMWF is the 700mb temperatures associated with this system. The ECMWF is much warmer than the GFS, keeping 700mb temperatures around -4 to -2C range, with a brief period of -5C. The GFS, however, suggests a cold system with a longer duration of -5C temperatures across southern portions of the region. Both long range models suggest that some snow would be likely, especially in the overnight hours, with this system, but the GFS evolution would likely produce more snow, given the longer duration of colder temperatures. This evolution will continue to be monitored over the upcoming model runs, to start getting a better idea of storm evolution and precipitation totals. Despite this, cooler temperatures are expected to return for much of next week.

GJT.name: Grand Junction
GJT.excerpt: As flow turns southwesterly ahead of a PacNW low, moisture begins its return to the region. The first signs of this pattern shift are expected on Friday as isolated storms will begin to pop up, though at this point QPF should be on the minimal side.

sections.name: Key Messages
paragraphs: - Monday through Thursday is expected to be mostly dry with another impactful system possible by the weekend.
- Model guidance reflects some uncertainty in storm tracks, leading to inconsistencies in moisture and river volume forecasts.

sections.name: Discussion
paragraphs: Near-zonal flow is established across the Intermountain West today, maintaining relatively dry conditions for our CWA. This keeps precipitation chances near-zero for most locations with little more than scattered cloud cover expected. We're sitting near-normal in terms of high temperatures as well, leaving valleys in the 50's to low-60's, and mountain locations in the 40's to low-50's. Though we continue to dry out steadily the next few days, some valley locations may still experience fog around sunrise which may impact morning commutes.
NEXT ROUND OF PRECIPITATION THIS WEEKEND:

As flow turns southwesterly ahead of a PacNW low, moisture begins its return to the region. The first signs of this pattern shift are expected on Friday as isolated storms will begin to pop up, though at this point QPF should be on the minimal side. By Sunday though, moisture will be hitting its peak in our CWA. As guidance stands there is little confidence in the exact trajectory of the broad moisture plume. If we are to lean one way or another, more evidence is suggesting that the strongest portion of the plume will pass to our south, though even in this scenario, southwestern Colorado is in line for yet another wet stretch with PWAT's up to 300% of normal. Adding to the complexity of this event is the progression of the upper-level pattern. As the PacNW low propagates eastwards towards the northern Rockies, a second low develops at the base of the trough, swinging through the southwestern portion of the county before eventually rejoining the parent trough early in the work week. The movement of both lows would likely have significant impacts on the nature of this storm system as temperatures will plummet to around 10 degrees below normal with their passage. This could be enough to drop snow level 1-2 kft. The complex pattern continues to lead to weak confidence in the timing and location of any eventual snowfall though, and as such we cannot yet speculate on how impacts will manifest from said snowfall. What we can say now though is that any notable amount of precipitation over southwestern Colorado locations recovering from last week's rainfall will have the potential to exacerbate flooding concerns. We are keeping a very close eye on this next round of precipitation as a result, and over the coming days as more details come into view we will begin to better gauge the risks Sunday into Monday morning. As such, stay tuned for additional information throughout this week. &&

PUB.name: Pueblo
PUB.excerpt: Long-range forecast remains consistent with recent model runs, though some of the fine details are still unclear. A broad upper trough will amplify over the Pacific Northwest, moving down the coast and tracking east through the weekend.

sections.name: Key Messages
paragraphs: - Drier and warmer through most of the week, with a pattern shift starting on Friday.
- Cooler and more active weather expected this weekend and into next week. Details remain uncertain.

sections.name: Short Term
paragraphs: With consistent fog across El Paso County, have issued a Dense Fog Advisory, valid through 9am today. Will monitor conditions to see if an expansion is needed.

Patchy fog is expected across the area into the morning hours. Take caution when traveling, as visibility could be reduced quickly. Main areas of concern will be areas along and east of I-25, along with the San Luis Valley. Conditions will improve by midday.
Generally a warm, dry day across the region today. High temperatures will be in the 60s to low-70s, with gradually clearing skies and light south winds.

Ongoing flooding will still be a concern around the Rio Grande and Conejos Rivers, with high flows and flood waters expected to linger for several more days. In addition, high flow continues to push through the Purgatoire River from recent rainfall, with minor flooding expected near Las Animas that will last through the day.

sections.name: Long Term
paragraphs: Warm and dry through most of the week. Temperatures will be 5-10 degrees above average around midweek, cooling a bit on Thursday after a passing wave shoves a dry cold front through the plains.

Long-range forecast remains consistent with recent model runs, though some of the fine details are still unclear. A broad upper trough will amplify over the Pacific Northwest, moving down the coast and tracking east through the weekend. Southwest flow will settle over our area out ahead of the system, with a renewed moisture tap leading to accumulating mountain snow starting on Friday. Beyond that, latest guidance has a low pressure system moving into our area later in the weekend, hinting at cooler and more unsettled weather into early next week. However, model solutions greatly diverge on the path and evolution of this system, so it will likely be several days before those details become certain.

SLC.name: Salt Lake City
SLC.excerpt: Behind the exiting system, a ridge is expected to develop off the Pacific coast, likely bringing an at least temporary end to the active pattern as of late.

sections.name: Key Messages
paragraphs: - Generally dry and seasonable conditions will persist through Thursday, with a weak grazing system tonight into Wednesday morning bringing a low chance of precipitation near the Utah/Idaho border.

- Moisture will increase over the area beginning Friday, bringing an increasing threat of flash flooding. The area will see a more substantial increase in moisture and instability and thus the potential for flooding Sunday into Monday as a strong Pacific storm crosses the area.
- Much cooler temperatures will accompany the system for early next week, allowing snow levels to potentially drop as low as 7500 feet by Monday morning.

sections.name: Discussion
paragraphs: Seeing a roughly zonal flow across Utah and southwest Wyoming this morning between an exit weak storm system and another Pacific Northwest storm system that will graze northern portions of the area tonight into Wednesday morning. Currently seeing mostly clear skies with some mid-level clouds near the Utah/Idaho border. Maxes today should run close to seasonal normals across the vast majority of the area.

With the passage of the next grazing system and associated front overnight, impacts should be similar to the one that just moved through. That is, the front will act to curb any warming trend and will bring a few showers near the Utah/Idaho border. Seasonable temperatures will continue through Thursday, with southerly flow gradually increasing.

Two storm system are expected to approach the Pacific coast Thursday, with the weaker southern one merging with the Pacific Northwest one by Friday. The southerly flow is expected to tap into some deeper moisture during the day Friday, with ejecting shortwaves out ahead of the main system providing additional instability. This will bring scattered showers and thunderstorms focused over southern Utah, bringing the potential for isolated flash flooding. Guidance overall is trending downward with coverage of precipitation with this part of the event, though at least some potential remains. In between systems, there should be a relative lull in convection on Saturday.

For Sunday, the previously mentioned Pacific Northwest storm system is expected to merge with a decaying tropical system before tracking across the area Sunday into Monday. The amount of moisture anticipated to accompany the system should be near records for this time of year, with the potent system and its strong associated cold front providing additional lift. This should bring widespread coverage of precipitation across utah and southwest Wyoming during the day Sunday, and given how saturated soils already are across southern Utah from the previous tropical events as of late, additional heavy rain has the potential to be that much more impactful. It should be noted, however, that this system is expected to be more progressive in nature than previous events and the associated precipitation a bit more steady in nature, providing a little bit in the way of limiting factors.

Given its Pacific Northwest origin, this system will also bring much colder air into the region, resulting in temperatures averaging 10-15F below seasonal normals to start the upcoming week. This influx of cold air will steadily lower snow levels through Monday morning, with a high chance of those snow levels moving into the 7000 to 8000 ft range.
Behind the exiting system, a ridge is expected to develop off the Pacific coast, likely bringing an at least temporary end to the active pattern as of late.

2755.travel_advice: Watch for signs of unstable snow such as recent avalanches, cracking in the snow, and audible collapsing. Avoid traveling on or under similar slopes.

product.author: Jason Konigsberg
bottom_line: Heavy rain on Wednesday and Thursday triggered small wet avalanches in the west-Central and Southern Mountains, but this concern is waning as temperatures drop. The most likely place to trigger an avalanche is at the highest elevations (above about 12,500 feet) in the Southern and west-Central Mountains on west, north, and east-facing slopes where new snow has been accumulating and a layer of mid-October snow persists. The Northern Mountains remain mostly bare.

This weekend, a new storm will deliver 4 to 8 inches of snow to the San Juan and Sangre de Cristo Mountains, creating fresh avalanche concerns on upper-elevation, wind-drifted slopes facing west, north, and east. Early-season travelers, including hunters and hikers, should use caution on steep terrain because even shallow snow on grassy slopes, rock slabs, or old snowfields can slide.

We will provide updates as needed until our daily forecasts resume on November 1, 2026. Please continue submitting your field observations, and check our website for real-time weather station data and model forecasts.

product.author: Kevin Studley
hazard_discussion: Avalanche Forecasting Operations Have Come to a Close for the 2026-26 Season
Have a safe spring in the mountains. Continue to remain vigilant and flexible while traveling in the mountains this spring.
OBSERVATIONS

Observations are still greatly appreciated. Spring-time observations are extremely helpful as forecast operations have come to a close. If you're out in the mountains, submit an observation to let the rest of the public know what's going on out there. Even a simple weather observation can be very useful.
• View recent observations HERE
• Submit an observation HERE
• Recent photos and videos HERE
Snow and Avalanche Information
• Dry Slab avalanche problems such as storm slab and wind slab avalanches are most likely during and immediately following a storm.

• Wet Loose avalanches are expected during warmups and (even brief) clear, sunny weather events, and rain events. Watch for pinwheels and rollerballs as an indicator the snow is becoming damp. If you're sinking into soft, mushy snow, it's time to turn around or find a different aspect.

• Wet Slab avalanches become likely during rain events and with multiple nights above freezing. Wet slabs occur when melt water pools and lubricates crusts or older persistent weak layers. Wet slab avalanches are notoriously difficult to predict.
• Cornices are large and often become unstable during prolonged warmups. Give yourself plenty of space above and below them. They tend to begin shedding during warming and/or rain events.
• Dry Loose Snow avalanches are expected during and immediately after a storm, particularly on shaded, north-facing slopes.

• Glide avalanches typically fail in similar spots year after year after an abundance of meltwater has saturated the ground or lower snowpack. Glide avalanches can occur in steep terrain, on smooth grassy slopes or on large slabs of rock. Look for glide cracks opening up during spring.
WEATHER
• Click HERE to view our Weather Station Map page with updated webcams
• Click HERE to view our Weather Tools page
• Spring weather patterns are often erratic and snow conditions can change quickly during spring weather. Be attentive to these changes and remain flexible with your travel plans.
• Rain on snow events can create dangerous avalanche conditions in a short period of time.
• Spring time means a higher sun angle, with direct solar radiation on the snowpack. Even a brief dose of sunshine can quickly alter the snow surface.

• Overcast skies and snow showers can open up to full sunshine in a matter of minutes. Convective snow showers can be spotty and difficult to forecast. Temperatures can vary depending on elevation and unexpected cloud cover can significantly alter a weather forecast.
OTHER CONSIDERATIONS
• Travel
• As people push into steeper, more consequential terrain, remember to maintain safe travel protocols and not let your guard down just because it's sunny and warm.
• During melt-freeze cycles, pay attention to "slide-for-life" circumstances, particularly during morning travel.
• Be mindful of terrain selection and timing. Identify terrain traps and be prepared to avoid/manage them.
• Spring Mindset

• Springtime is when mountain travelers push for bigger objectives. We have greater confidence in the stability of the snowpack and the high sun angle makes us feel ready to charge. As we start stepping out into bigger terrain in the mountains, be mindful of consequences (ask yourself, "If this slides, what will happen?"). Choose your terrain appropriately and manage new/surface snow problems accordingly. Be aware that dynamic weather can have quick impacts on the snow surface. A common theme I've noticed over the last 15 years playing in steep, snowy mountains is that experienced, seasoned people often get caught in small avalanches in big terrain during the spring. We have a tendency to underestimate "manageable" new snow problems like wind slab and loose snow. Pay attention to changing weather and know that small shifts in spring weather can have dramatic impacts on the upper snowpack.

(Precipitation data are recorded from Secesh SNOTEL site at 6540')
